---

Strapped to the bed of circumcision lies
My son. This mutilation binds
You to the fathers. Never will they let
You forget, nor your flesh be enfranchised,
Though you pray your whole life long.
Early they set you on the rack, and infect you with a fever
Of remembrance. In the marriage bed,
When you lie naked, there the sign burns red.
There is neither meeting nor mating, only the past
Crying that you were promised, wed already—
I will not bless this mark upon your body.
For you the hurricane rises fast;
I feel the horns of Moses pressing at my brow,
And Law wrenched once more from the dead
Hand of deity—and I descend out of the storm to you,
Mad with loneliness upon this bed.

Yet I hold in reserve that rage
Which once broke the Law upon you like a rain of stone,
That other time I watched you yearn so.
The Law lies broken, child. I will not ascend again.

---

# On the Circumcision of My Son

The infant boy lies beneath the ritual blade, too small to understand what is being written into his flesh this day. What passes for a covenant, I see instead as a form of mutilation—ancient, sanctioned, and utterly binding. With this cut, he is claimed. He is sealed irrevocably to the long chain of fathers before him, to a tradition that reaches back through centuries of blood and ash, demanding his allegiance before he has even learned to speak his own name.

I cannot escape the knowledge that this marking is permanent. It will not fade with time, nor will it loosen its grip as the boy grows into a man. His flesh will never know what it means to be simply *free*—unenfranchised from this history, unmarked by the weight of inheritance. Even in his most private moments, even in the marriage bed where a man might expect some sanctuary of self, this sign will be present, an old testimony written on his body that speaks before he does, that announces him as belonging to something vast and demanding, whether he chooses it or not.

And so I will not offer my blessing. Let others praise this rite as sacred; I see it instead as a *fever of remembering* imposed upon a child too young to consent—a lifelong communion with suffering he did not choose, a tether to a past whose pain outweighs whatever meaning tradition claims to offer. To bless this would be to pretend that inherited anguish is a gift, and I cannot make that pretense.

The image comes to me of Moses upon the mountain, the Law torn from the dead hand of a deity whose commandments have outlived their mercy—stone tablets inscribed not with liberation but with obligation, passed down not as choice but as decree. I stand caught in that ancient tension, between reverence for what my fathers believed and this anguish at watching it repeat itself in the body of my own son. I did not ask for this inheritance, and yet here I am, complicit, watching it happen again.

But something in me refuses. I feel a rage rising—not loud, not righteous, but deep and certain—against this Law that claims dominion over flesh not yet capable of understanding sacrifice. I declare it *broken*. I will not climb that mountain again to receive what was handed down; I will not *ascend* to accept commandments carved by hands long dead, insisting still on obedience from the living. Let this be my quiet rebellion: to love my son fully while refusing the framework that says his body must first be claimed before it can be his own.
outputs.L4:
**The Eighth Day**

They came with the small silver knife
wrapped in linen older than my grandfather's name,
and I stood in the doorway of that room
where light fell through the blinds like the bars
of some ancient scripture, unreadable now
except in the language of blood.

My son. Small fists closed around nothing,
around the air that hadn't yet
learned to carry his name. I thought of Moses
in the reeds, his mother's hands trembling
the same tremble mine held now—
that current passed down like water
finding the same crack in stone
generation after generation,
wearing the body into covenant
whether the body agrees or not.

They say Abraham took the knife himself.
They say the angel stayed his hand for Isaac
but not for this—not for the flesh
that binds son to father to father's father,
back through the wilderness, through Egypt,
through every threshold marked in blood
so the angel of death might pass over.
But what if I want the angel to stop here?
What if I am tired of building doorframes
out of my child's body?

I have read the tablets. I have felt
their weight in my own chest since childhood,
the Law they say was carved by God's own finger—
but whose finger guides the knife today?
Whose voice says *this is what love looks like*,
this cutting, this letting, this small covenant
of pain we call belonging?

I looked at my son's face, unmarked
by anything but sleep, and thought:
*This is where it could end.*
Not out of doubt in what came before—
the burning bush, the parting sea,
the years of wandering that made a people
out of scattered slaves—
but because inheritance is not obligation.
Because a mark is not a meaning
until we make it one.

So when the mohel raised his hands
and waited for my blessing,
I said nothing.
I would not call this holy.
I would not say the words
that turn a wound into a covenant,
that turn my silence into complicity
with every father before me
who did not ask, who did not stop,
who only passed the knife
like a torch through fields of wheat,
burning as it went.

The Law, I said—not to the room,
not even to my son, but to the ghosts
that gathered in the corners like dust—
*The Law is broken.*
Not shattered, not destroyed,
but broken like a fever breaks,
like a chain finally corroded through
by all the tears that fell on it
for thousands of years, unnoticed,
mistaken for devotion.

I will not bless this cutting.
I will not call this belonging.
Let him be his own covenant—
let his body write its own testament,
unscarred by my forefathers' hunger
for a God who needed proof
carved into every generation's skin.

Let the angel pass over
without needing blood on the doorpost.
Let this be the last house
it visits for that reason.

I held my son that night
the way water holds its own reflection—
not master of it, not separate from it,
but momentarily, fiercely
whole.
outputs.L5:
# Strapped

You know this feeling. The one where the calendar becomes a countdown—not to something exciting, but to the next paycheck, the next bill, the next moment you have to say "not right now" to something you actually want.

Being strapped for cash isn't just about numbers in a bank account. It's the mental tax you pay every single day. This constant calculation running in the background: *Can I afford this? Should I skip that? What happens if something breaks?*

This is the reality for millions of people, and if you're reading this because it resonates with you, know that you're not alone in it—even though it can feel profoundly isolating.

There's a particular exhaustion that comes with being financially strapped. It's not just about deprivation; it's about the vigilance. You become hyperaware of prices, of due dates, of the gap between what you have and what you need. This awareness never fully switches off, even when you're trying to relax, trying to sleep, trying to just exist without the weight of arithmetic pressing on your chest.

But this state, however suffocating, is rarely permanent. Circumstances shift. Opportunities appear. What feels unbearable this month may look different in six.

If you find yourself strapped right now, this much is true: acknowledging the difficulty is not weakness. It's honest. And that honesty—with yourself, and sometimes with others—can be the first step toward loosening the grip this situation has on you.

You are more than your bank balance. This moment, however hard, doesn't define your worth or your future. It's simply where you are right now—not where you'll always be.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, intense free-verse poem about a father's ambivalence during his newborn son's circumcision ceremony, weaving in imagery of Moses and the breaking of the Law.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Eighth Day**

They hand him to me wrapped like a scroll not yet unrolled,
his mouth already fluent in the language of complaint.
I hold my son the way Moses must have held
the tablets before he understood what breaking meant—

that some words are written to be shattered,
that covenant sometimes needs a wound to prove itself real.

Downstairs, the men are sharpening a mercy.
The mohel's hands are steady as a verdict.
I think of Zipporah kneeling in the dark,
flint knife flashing like an accusation,
the bridegroom of blood she made her husband,
covenant paid in a currency of foreskin
before Pharaoh ever heard the word *let*.

What Law is this that enters through the body first?
What God needs proof written in an infant's flesh
before the mind can consent to anything?

I want to be Moses parting some water,
carrying my son through on dry ground,
sparing him this early Egypt of the blade.
I want to smash the tablets on the altar table,
scatter commandment into desert dust,
say *no*, say *not this one*, say *let him stay unwritten*.

But I am already lifting him toward the men,
already a father performing fatherhood's oldest contradiction—
to promise protection with one hand
while the other signs him over to the tribe,
to make of my son's small cry
a kind of psalm, a kind of law,
the ancient wound that says: *you belong to something older than your pain.*

The blade does what blades do.
He screams the scream of all beginnings.
Blood, wine, someone's blessing murmured like an apology.

I think: *this is how we ratify our belonging—
in flesh, in flinching, in the moment just after breaking
when what's broken becomes what's sacred.*

I think: *forgive me, I did not part any sea for you.*

I carry him back upstairs, already sealed,
already scarred into a story he'll never remember choosing,
his small body a testament
written in the oldest ink there is.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the voice of a conflicted parent watching a bris, blending religious tradition, resentment toward inherited faith, and the biblical Moses narrative.
counterfactuals.output:
**Eighth Day**

They pass him to the sandek's knees
the way Jochebed lowered a basket to the current—
*here, take him, let the river decide
what nation claims his name.*

I stand where Pharaoh's daughter might have stood,
half in the water, half out,
watching a child not fully mine
become the property of covenant.

The mohel lays out silver instruments
and I count them like plagues:
one for the blood, one for the wine,
one for the blessing I mouth
without believing,
because my father taught me the words
before he taught me why,
and his father did the same,
back to some man in a desert
who heard a voice in fire
and said *who am I*
and was answered anyway,
never given the choice
he asked for.

I wanted to give my son a choice.
Instead I give him a name
whispered over wine-wet lips,
a scar he'll wear before he can spell his own history,
a covenant cut into him
like a river carving the only shape
it was ever going to make.

The women hum something old.
The uncles argue in low voices
about whether the blessing was fast enough, right enough—
as if God is a stopwatch,
as if my resentment isn't also a kind of prayer,
the only one I have left:
*let him forgive me
for the tradition I couldn't refuse
and didn't want to,
for handing him downriver
the way it was handed to me,
half rescue, half surrender,
until he's old enough
to stand at his own water's edge
and decide.*

The baby cries—thin, furious, alive.
Someone says *mazel tov.*
I say nothing,
watching the blood already becoming story,
the boy already becoming
someone I both made
and cannot own,
a small ark
sent out
before I was ready
to let him go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a raw, emotionally charged poem about circumcision as both covenant and wound, using allusions to Moses, the Ten Commandments, and Mount Sinai's imagery of thunder and stone.
counterfactuals.output:
# Eighth Day

The knife descended like the tablets fell,
not broken this time, but breaking me in—
a covenant carved into what I cannot tell
my son when he asks where the story begins.

They say Moses came down with thunder in his hands,
that God spoke fire into shapes of law,
that the mountain shook until it cracked its bands
and something holy passed through something raw.

I was eight days old and knew nothing of Sinai,
nothing of smoke or trumpet-blast or flame—
only the small apocalypse, the private cry,
the blood that sealed me into someone's name.

They call it covenant. I call it the first wound
that taught me love and law can wear the same face,
that promises get written when the flesh is ruined,
that belonging leaves a scar in every place

it enters. Abraham took the blade himself—
imagine that, a father's hand, the cut,
the ancient bargain kept like something on a shelf
that history keeps taking down, keeps shutting

into skin instead of stone. I have no tablets,
no mountain trembling with a voice of fire,
just this quiet body bearing what it cannot settle—
whether wound is worship, or worship just a wire

stretched between the wanting and the given.
Thunder doesn't ask the rock's permission
to become commandment. I was young. Unwritten.
Now I carry law I never chose, a sacred incision

that says: you are mine, you are marked, you are other,
you belong to something older than your name—
the way Moses belonged to God, and not his mother,
the way the mountain wasn't just a mountain, but a flame

that had to burn something to prove it burned at all.
I don't know if I believe in what was done to me.
I only know the blood, the knife, the fall
into meaning I didn't ask for, but cannot flee—

covenant and wound wearing the same skin,
thunder and scar telling the same old story:
that to belong to God is to let something in
that cuts first, and calls the cutting glory.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modern confessional poem exploring the pain and rage of passing down religious tradition to a son through circumcision, ending with a rejection of the sacred Law.
counterfactuals.output:
**Eighth Day**

They said bring him in white, unmarked,
say the blessing before the blood,
so I stood in my father's suit
that never fit either of us
and watched a stranger's hands
find the exact place
where covenant meets skin.

Someone gave him wine
before he had a word for thirst.
Someone held his legs
the way I once was held —
my grandfather's thumb
pressed into my grandfather's father's
same old law, a chain
of small blades passed down
like heirlooms
nobody asked to inherit.

I did not look away. That's the confession —
I made myself watch
because my father watched,
because his father stood
in some other kitchen, some other decade,
holding his coat closed
against the same eight-day cold,
and none of us said *no,*
none of us said *this hurts him*
though the room was thick with proof.

Abraham took a knife up a mountain
for less than this.
I keep thinking of the ram
that showed up just in time —
how it never shows up in time
for the rest of us,
how somebody still bleeds
so a story can go on being holy.

My son's cry filled the small room
like an accusation
in a language older
than any word for *stop.*
I held the cup they gave me,
sweet wine, a symbolic mouth,
and thought: I am handing him
a wound and calling it belonging,
making him a promise
he never made, in a voice
that isn't his, that isn't even
fully mine.

Here is what I know now,
written line by line into my palms:
the Law was never about the body.
It was about obedience
dressed up as love,
pain made permanent
so no one could leave the room
without some evidence they'd stayed.

So let this be my heresy —
plain as a table with no cloth on it.
I will not call the scar sacred.
I will not tell him God required proof
that he belonged to anyone.
I take back the mountain, the ram,
the knife I never held but chose.

Whatever covenant is left between us,
let it be the one uncut —
let it be only this:
my hand, open, empty,
his.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, symbolic poem about a father refusing to bless his son's circumcision, using Old Testament imagery (Moses, the tablets of Law, sacrifice) to express personal rebellion against inherited faith.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Unbroken Covenant

I stood where Moses stood, but would not kneel—
the mountain smoking still with someone else's fire,
the tablets offered like a knife wrapped in wool.
*Take this*, they said. *It is only what was always yours.*

But whose hands carved the letters into stone?
Not mine. I did not choose the wilderness,
did not ask for forty years to wander
in a story that began before my name.

My son sleeps in the next room, unmarked,
his small body a page no one has written on yet.
They want me to be Abraham on the mountain,
to raise the blade because a voice once spoke
from a bush that burned but was not consumed.

I say: let it be consumed.
Let the bush burn down to root and ash.
I will not lift my hand.
I will not be the angel's alibi.

There is a covenant older than circumcision—
the one between a father and the softness
of his son's untouched skin, the one
that says *I will not pass this wound to you
simply because it was passed to me.*

Let the rabbis weep. Let the fathers
who came before me turn their faces
like pillars of salt, frozen
in the act of looking back.

I am standing at the parting of a different sea.
On one side: Egypt, and the God of my fathers,
and the knife that makes belonging out of blood.
On the other: nothing. No pillar of cloud.
No manna falling like a promise.
Just my son, and my refusal,
and the terrible freedom
of a covenant I choose to end.

Let the tablets shatter at the mountain's foot.
Let them stay unread.
I will write no law into his flesh
that I did not first write in my own bones—
and I have written *no*.
I have written *not this time*.
I have written: *the sacrifice stops here,
with me,
the ram already tangled in the thicket,
already, gratefully, unkilled.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
